items.title: Legal powers and judicial review
items.body: A public body can only do what the law allows it to do. Its powers come from statute, and acting outside them is called ultra vires. Some powers are broad: English local authorities, for example, have a general power of competence under the Localism Act 2011, but it cannot be used to override other laws. Decisions can be challenged in court by judicial review. The main grounds are illegality (wrong law or no power), irrationality (a decision no reasonable body could make) and procedural unfairness (such as not consulting when required or not hearing the other side). Before starting a new service, the team should be able to point to the power or duty it relies on and record it in the decision.

questions.prompt: What does it mean if a public body acts ultra vires?

options.text: It acts beyond its legal powers
It spends more than its budget
It acts without telling the press
A review of a judge's decision by a colleague
A court process that checks whether a public body's decision was lawful
An audit of a court's accounts

questions.prompt: Which is a ground for judicial review?
A council wants to launch a new service but nobody can say which power allows it. What do you do before going ahead?
questions.answer: Get legal advice and identify the statutory power or duty relied on (for example a specific Act, or the general power of competence where it applies), check it does not conflict with other law, and record the legal basis in the decision report. If there is no power, do not proceed.
questions.rubric: Should require legal advice, identification of the specific power or duty, checking limits and conflicts with other law, and recording the legal basis. Must not proceed without a power.

items.title: The Public Sector Equality Duty
items.body: Section 149 of the Equality Act 2010 requires public authorities, when carrying out their functions, to have due regard to three aims: eliminating discrimination, harassment and victimisation; advancing equality of opportunity between people who share a protected characteristic and those who do not; and fostering good relations between them. There are nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation. Due regard must be paid in substance and with an open mind, before the decision is made, not as a box-ticking exercise afterwards. An equality impact assessment is the usual way to show it: who is affected, what the evidence says, how the proposal could be changed to reduce harm, and how the effect will be monitored.

questions.prompt: Which section of the Equality Act 2010 sets the Public Sector Equality Duty?
Which is one of the three aims of the equality duty?
How many protected characteristics are there under the Equality Act 2010?
When should an equality impact assessment be done and what should a good one contain?
questions.answer: Early, while options are still open and before a decision is made, and updated as plans change. It sets out who is affected, the evidence used, the likely positive and negative effects for each protected group, how harm can be avoided or reduced, any consultation, and how the effect will be monitored. It is considered by the decision makers.
questions.rubric: Must say: before the decision, while options are open. Content: who is affected, evidence, effects by protected group, mitigation, consultation, monitoring. Credit for saying decision makers must consider it and that it is not a retrospective exercise.

items.title: Consultation, human rights and subsidy control
items.source: R v Brent LBC ex p Gunning (1985); Human Rights Act 1998; Subsidy Control Act 2022
items.body: When a public body consults, the courts expect it to follow four principles known as the Gunning principles. Consultation takes place when proposals are still at a formative stage. Enough information is given for people to respond properly. People have adequate time to respond. And the decision makers conscientiously consider the responses before deciding. Separately, section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998 makes it unlawful for a public authority to act in a way that is incompatible with the Convention rights. And when a public authority gives financial help that could distort competition to an enterprise, such as a grant or a discounted lease, the Subsidy Control Act 2022 sets rules and principles that must be checked first.

questions.prompt: At what point should a public body consult on a proposal?

options.text: After the decision has been made
Only when asked to by the press
While proposals are still at a formative stage
Once the contract has been signed

questions.prompt: What does section 6 of the Human Rights Act 1998 say about public authorities?

options.text: They are exempt from human rights law
They need not consider rights during emergencies
It is unlawful for them to act incompatibly with Convention rights

questions.prompt: Which law sets the rules when a council wants to give a grant to a private company?
A three-week consultation on closing a service gets mostly negative responses. The decision makers go ahead without reading them. What is wrong and what is the risk?
questions.answer: The decision makers must conscientiously consider the responses. The time may also be too short for the proposal, and the information may not have been sufficient. Not considering the responses breaches the Gunning principles and exposes the decision to judicial review. The remedy is to read and analyse the responses, report them to the decision makers, show how they influenced the outcome and revisit the equality assessment.
questions.rubric: Should say the responses must be conscientiously considered (Gunning), may mention adequate time and information, risk of judicial review, and the remedy: analyse, report to decision makers, show influence, revisit EIA.

items.title: Accessibility, complaints and legal change
items.source: Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018
items.body: Public sector websites and apps must meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines at level AA and publish an accessibility statement that explains what does not yet comply and when it will be fixed. A complaints policy should be easy to find, say who handles a complaint and how long it takes, and explain what to do if the person is still unhappy; for English councils the next step is the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman. Laws, regulations and guidance change, so someone should own a simple legal watch that tracks what affects the service and when. When a service closes, some duties continue: records must be kept for the retention period, personal data is protected, and information requests still apply to what is held.

questions.prompt: What must public sector websites publish about accessibility?

options.text: A list of all disabled users
An accessibility statement explaining any gaps and plans to fix them
The contract with the web developer

questions.prompt: Which body can look at complaints about English councils after the council's own process has finished?

options.text: The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman

questions.prompt: Why should a service keep a legal change watch?

options.text: To avoid ever changing the service
Because it is required for every email
Laws and guidance change, and the service must stay compliant

questions.prompt: A programme is closing. Which legal duties continue after closure and how would you plan for them?
questions.answer: Records must be kept for their retention period and then reviewed or destroyed properly. Personal data stays protected under data protection law. Information requests still apply to information held. Contract liabilities, staff matters and any archived web content accessibility may also continue. Name an owner for each duty and record it in the closure plan.
questions.rubric: Should list continuing duties such as records retention, data protection, information requests, contract and staff liabilities, accessibility of archived content, and assign owners in the closure plan.
